fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.name: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.summary: Sixth Fatimid caliph and sixteenth Ismaili imam (985-1021), a deeply controversial ruler seen by some as a tyrant and by others as an ideal, divinely ordained sovereign.

mulukhiyah.name: Mulukhiyah
mulukhiyah.summary: A traditional Egyptian and Arab dish made from the leaves of a jute plant, cooked into a thick, mucilaginous broth or stew and usually served with rice.

al-zahir-li-i-zaz-din-allah.name: Al-Zahir li-I'zaz Din Allah
al-zahir-li-i-zaz-din-allah.summary: Seventh Fatimid Imam-caliph (1021–1036), who succeeded his father al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah after his disappearance.

arab-conquest-of-egypt.name: Arab conquest of Egypt
arab-conquest-of-egypt.summary: The Rashidun Caliphate's conquest of Byzantine Egypt between 639 and 642 AD, ending nearly a thousand years of Greco-Roman rule there.

ful-medames.name: Ful medames
ful-medames.summary: A stew of cooked fava beans seasoned with olive oil and spices, considered Egypt's national dish and a staple food there since at least the 17th century.

corchorus-olitorius.name: Corchorus olitorius
corchorus-olitorius.summary: A shrub also known as jute mallow or Jew's mallow, whose leaves are eaten as a vegetable and whose fiber is a primary source of jute.

alodia.name: Alodia
alodia.summary: Medieval Christian kingdom in what is now central Sudan, with its capital at Soba, that thrived as a multicultural trading hub roughly from the 6th century until around 1500.

makuria.name: Makuria
makuria.summary: Medieval Nubian kingdom, capital Dongola, in what is now northern Sudan and southern Egypt; it repelled an Arab invasion in 652 and kept a resulting peace treaty for six centuries.

abd-al-latif-al-baghdadi.name: Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi
abd-al-latif-al-baghdadi.summary: A physician, philosopher, historian, Arabic grammarian and traveller from Baghdad, living from 1162 to 1231, and one of the most prolific writers of his time.

ibn-iyas.name: Muhammad ibn Iyas
ibn-iyas.summary: An eyewitness historian of the Ottoman conquest of Egypt (1448–1522/4), born and educated in Cairo, whose accounts of Mamluk rulers are widely quoted.

bab-zuwayla.name: Bab Zuweila
bab-zuwayla.summary: One of three surviving gates in the walls of historic Cairo, built in 1092, with its twin minarets added in the 15th century alongside the Mosque of Sultan al-Muayyad.

saladin.name: Saladin
saladin.summary: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and first sultan of Egypt and Syria (c. 1137 to 1193), who led the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states during the Third Crusade.

cairo-citadel.name: Cairo Citadel
cairo-citadel.summary: A medieval fortress begun by Saladin in 1176, serving as the seat of Egypt's rulers for nearly 700 years until the 19th century.

al-kamil.name: Al-Kamil
al-kamil.summary: Egyptian ruler and fourth Ayyubid sultan of Egypt (c. 1177-1238) who defeated the Fifth Crusade and later ceded West Jerusalem to the Christians during the Sixth Crusade.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

nobatia.name: Nobatia
nobatia.summary: A late antique kingdom in Lower Nubia, in what is now southern Egypt, that succeeded Kush; founded around 400, it converted to Coptic Christianity in 543 and was later annexed by Makuria.

faras.name: Faras
faras.summary: A major city in Lower Nubia, on the border of modern Egypt and Sudan, now permanently flooded by Lake Nasser after extensive archaeological excavation.

copts.name: Copts
copts.summary: A Christian ethnoreligious group native to Egypt, descended from the ancient Egyptians, historically speaking the Coptic language and now the largest Christian population in the Middle East.

ayyubid-dynasty.name: Ayyubid dynasty
ayyubid-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin founded by Saladin in 1171, which ruled Egypt and much of Syria until its own Mamluk soldiers overthrew it in 1250.

mausoleum-of-imam-al-shafi-i.name: Mausoleum of Imam al-Shafi'i
mausoleum-of-imam-al-shafi-i.summary: A tomb complex in Cairo's City of the Dead honoring al-Shafi'i, founder of a major school of Sunni Islamic law, first built over his grave by the Ayyubid sultan Saladin in 1176.

city-of-the-dead-cairo.name: Southern Cemetery
city-of-the-dead-cairo.summary: The older southern section of Cairo's vast Islamic-era necropolis, holding graves and elaborate mausoleums and part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Cairo.

old-dongola.name: Old Dongola
old-dongola.summary: A now-deserted Nubian town on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the medieval kingdom of Makuria from the 4th to 14th century, later replaced by modern Dongola downstream.

baqt.name: Baqt
baqt.summary: A 7th-century treaty between the Christian Nubian kingdom of Makuria and the Muslim rulers of Egypt, reputedly the longest-lasting treaty in history, lasting nearly 700 years.

qutuz.name: Qutuz
qutuz.summary: Mamluk Sultan of Egypt who reigned less than a year (1259–1260) but led the Mamluk army to a decisive victory over the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, then was assassinated on the journey home.

hulegu-khan.name: Hulegu Khan
hulegu-khan.summary: Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265) and grandson of Genghis Khan who conquered much of West Asia, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia, and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid dynasty.

battle-of-ain-jalut.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
battle-of-ain-jalut.summary: A battle fought on 3 September 1260 near the spring of Ain Jalut in Galilee, where the Mamluks of Egypt defeated the Mongol Ilkhanate's army, marking the first major halt to Mongol expansion.

baybars.name: Baybars
baybars.summary: The fourth Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria (1260-1277), a former slave who defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut and campaigned successfully against the Crusaders.

baldwin-iv-of-jerusalem.name: Baldwin IV
baldwin-iv-of-jerusalem.summary: King of Jerusalem from 1174 to 1185, known as the Leper King; crowned at thirteen despite his illness, he fought to contain Saladin while managing court infighting and the succession.

battle-of-montgisard.name: Battle of Montgisard
battle-of-montgisard.summary: A 25 November 1177 battle in which Baldwin IV of Jerusalem, though afflicted with leprosy, routed Saladin's Egyptian army, one of the Crusades' most notable engagements.

david-of-makuria.name: David of Makuria
david-of-makuria.summary: King of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, reigning from 1268 or 1269 until his death on 4 June 1276.

aydhab.name: ʿAydhab
aydhab.summary: A now-abandoned medieval port on the Red Sea's western coast, in territory today disputed between Egypt and Sudan.

beit-she-an.name: Beit She'an
beit-she-an.summary: One of the region's oldest cities, at a key junction in Israel's Jordan Valley, known through history as Scythopolis and later, in Arabic, as Beisan or Bisan.

kitbuqa.name: Kitbuqa
kitbuqa.summary: An Eastern Christian Naiman general who served the Mongol Ilkhan Hulagu, helping sack Baghdad in 1258, and was killed in 1260 at the Battle of Ain Jalut, the first major defeat of Mongol expansion.

louis-ix-of-france.name: Louis IX of France
louis-ix-of-france.summary: King of France from 1226 to 1270, also known as Saint Louis and the sole French king canonised as a Catholic saint. He led the Seventh and Eighth Crusades and was captured and ransomed during the Seventh.

seventh-crusade.name: Seventh Crusade
seventh-crusade.summary: A crusade (1248-1254) led by Louis IX of France against Egypt to reclaim the Holy Land, ending in defeat and the capture of much of the army, including the king.

damietta.name: Damietta
damietta.summary: A port city in Egypt's Nile Delta, about 200 km north of Cairo and 15 km from the Mediterranean, and historically a Catholic bishopric.

as-salih-ayyub.name: As-Salih Ayyub
as-salih-ayyub.summary: Ayyubid ruler of Egypt from 1240 to 1249.

shajar-al-durr.name: Shajar al-Durr
shajar-al-durr.summary: A ruler of Egypt of Turkic origin who became sultana in 1250 after her husband died during the Seventh Crusade, ending Ayyubid rule and beginning the Mamluk era.

faris-al-din-aktay.name: Faris al-Din Aktay
faris-al-din-aktay.summary: Turkic-Kipchak emir and leader of the Bahri Mamluks who died in Cairo in 1254.

hasankeyf.name: Hasankeyf
hasankeyf.summary: A town on the Tigris in Batman Province, Turkey, whose historic town and archaeological sites were flooded by the Ilısu Dam project by 2020.

raynald-of-ch-tillon.name: Raynald of Châtillon
raynald-of-ch-tillon.summary: A crusader lord (c.1124 to 1187) who was Prince of Antioch and later Lord of Transjordan, known for plundering raids and for leading the crusader army that defeated Saladin as regent in 1177.

ascalon.name: Ascalon
ascalon.summary: An ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast of the southern Levant, settled from the 3rd millennium BCE and fought over for centuries, including two major Crusader battles in 1099 and 1153.

kingdom-of-al-abwab.name: Kingdom of al-Abwab
kingdom-of-al-abwab.summary: A medieval Nubian kingdom in present-day central Sudan, initially a province of Alodia that became independent around 1268, later drawn into wars between Makuria and the Mamluk sultanate.

al-mufaddal-ibn-abi-al-fada-il.name: al-Mufaddal ibn Abi al-Fada'il
al-mufaddal-ibn-abi-al-fada-il.summary: A 14th-century Coptic Christian Egyptian historian who wrote a detailed chronicle of Egypt and Syria, including the Mongol occupation, finished in 1358, and also covered the Horn of Africa.

al-nasir-muhammad.name: al-Nasir Muhammad
al-nasir-muhammad.summary: Ninth Mamluk sultan of the Bahri dynasty, ruling Egypt across three reigns between 1293 and 1341, who reformed taxation and appointed loyal officials to fight corruption.

abdallah-barshanbu.name: Abdallah Barshanbu
abdallah-barshanbu.summary: King of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria from 1316 to 1317, the first Muslim ruler of the Christian kingdom, installed by the Mamluks and killed within a year.

ibn-al-farid.name: Ibn al-Farid
ibn-al-farid.summary: Arab Sufi poet (1181–1234), born and died in Cairo. His poetry was admired across Arabic and Persian speaking regions, and Persian poets such as Jami wrote commentaries on it.

al-azhar-university.name: Al-Azhar University
al-azhar-university.summary: Founded in Cairo in 970 by the Fatimid Caliphate, it is Egypt's oldest university and one of the most prestigious centers of Islamic learning in the world.

maimonides.name: Maimonides
maimonides.summary: Sephardic Jewish rabbi (c. 1135/38-1204) widely seen as one of the most influential Torah scholars of the Middle Ages, who also served as physician to Saladin.

coptic-language.name: Coptic language
coptic-language.summary: The last stage of the Egyptian language, spoken from the 3rd century AD and written in the Coptic alphabet; replaced by Arabic but still used in church liturgy.

al-azhar-mosque.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
al-azhar-mosque.summary: Mosque in Cairo, dedicated in 972, and the first built in the new Fatimid capital. Its affiliated university is the second oldest continuously run in the world and a leading centre for Sunni theology and Islamic law.

ibn-al-nafis.name: Ibn al-Nafis
ibn-al-nafis.summary: An Arab polymath working in medicine, surgery and philosophy who was the first to describe pulmonary circulation of the blood, pre-dating William Harvey's 1628 work on the subject.

theologus-autodidactus.name: Theologus Autodidactus
theologus-autodidactus.summary: An Arabic novel written by Ibn al-Nafis between 1268 and 1277, considered one of the earliest Arabic novels, blending science fiction, a coming-of-age tale, and a desert island story.

ali-ibn-ridwan.name: Ali ibn Ridwan
ali-ibn-ridwan.summary: Arab physician, astrologer and astronomer in Egypt (c. 988–1061) known for the most detailed surviving account of the 1006 supernova, the brightest stellar event ever recorded.

sn-1006.name: SN 1006
sn-1006.summary: A supernova first observed in 1006, likely the brightest stellar event in recorded history, seen across China, Japan, Iraq, Egypt, and Europe.

najm-al-din-al-misri.name: Najm al-Din al-Misri
najm-al-din-al-misri.summary: A 14th-century Egyptian astronomer known for a vast astronomical table with nearly 415,000 entries and a treatise describing over 100 astronomical instruments.

ibn-yunus.name: Ibn Yunus
ibn-yunus.summary: An Arab-Egyptian astronomer and mathematician (c. 950–1009) given an observatory by the Fatimids, who compiled detailed astronomical tables during the reign of al-Hakim.

astrolabe.name: Astrolabe
astrolabe.summary: An ancient astronomical instrument and star chart used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies and to determine time, latitude, or position.

quadrans-vetus.name: Quadrans Vetus
quadrans-vetus.summary: Medieval astronomical instrument, the "old quadrant," used to measure heights, distances and depths; only three medieval examples survive today.

simon-newcomb.name: Simon Newcomb
simon-newcomb.summary: A Canadian-American astronomer, applied mathematician, and polymath (1835–1909) who made important contributions to timekeeping, as well as to economics and statistics.

pierre-simon-laplace.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
pierre-simon-laplace.summary: French polymath (1749–1827) whose work shaped physics, astronomy and mathematics, including the Laplace transform and early ideas resembling black holes.

axial-tilt.name: Obliquity of the ecliptic
axial-tilt.summary: The angle between a planet's rotational axis and the line perpendicular to its orbital plane, which causes the changing seasons.

bahri-mamluks.name: Bahri Mamluks
bahri-mamluks.summary: The ruling dynasty of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt from 1250 to 1382, mostly manumitted slave-soldiers of Turkic origin, succeeded by the Circassian Burji Mamluks.

al-ashraf-khalil.name: Al-Ashraf Khalil
al-ashraf-khalil.summary: Eighth Bahri Mamluk sultan of Egypt (1290-1293), famed for capturing Acre in 1291 and ending the last Crusader state in Palestine, before being assassinated.

acre-israel.name: Acre
acre-israel.summary: Coastal city in northern Israel with a natural harbour, continuously inhabited since the Bronze Age and a major Crusader stronghold until its fall in 1291.

al-adil-i.name: Al-Adil I
al-adil-i.summary: Fourth Sultan of Egypt and Syria (1145-1218) and brother of Saladin, a skilled administrator and general who helped found the Ayyubid dynasty.

barquq.name: Barquq
barquq.summary: First sultan of the Circassian Mamluk Burji dynasty of Egypt, ruling 1382–1389 and 1390–1399; born a Christian in Circassia, he was enslaved before rising to power.

burji-mamluks.name: Burji dynasty
burji-mamluks.summary: Circassian-origin ruling line of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt from 1382 to 1517, whose sultans were purchased as slaves and manumitted before taking power, ended by Ottoman conquest.

joel-of-makuria.name: Joel
joel-of-makuria.summary: A 15th-century king of Makuria, a Christian kingdom in Nubia, and one of the last kings of Christian Nubia known from historical records, surviving only in a few inscriptions and a 1484 letter.

qaitbay.name: Qaitbay
qaitbay.summary: Mamluk Sultan of Egypt from 1468 to 1496 who stabilized the state's economy, fought the Ottomans, and was a major patron of architecture across the region.

dotawo.name: Dotawo
dotawo.summary: A Christian kingdom in Lower Nubia during the Middle Ages, attested in documents from the 12th to 15th centuries as one of the last Christian states in the region.

fifth-crusade.name: Fifth Crusade
fifth-crusade.summary: A 1217-1221 campaign by Western Europeans to retake Jerusalem by first conquering Egypt's Ayyubid Sultanate, ending after early success at Damietta turned to failure near Cairo.

sixth-crusade.name: Sixth Crusade
sixth-crusade.summary: A 1228-1229 expedition led by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II that regained control of Jerusalem mainly through diplomacy rather than fighting.

frederick-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor
frederick-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of Sicily, Germany, Italy and Jerusalem, and Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 to 1250, ruling from Sicily to Germany and repeatedly clashing with the papacy, which excommunicated him four times.

gebel-adda.name: Gebel Adda
gebel-adda.summary: A mountain and archaeological site on the Nubian Nile in southern Egypt, inhabited from the 2nd to the late 18th century AD, that served as the likely capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria in the 14th and 15th centuries.

an-nasir-faraj.name: An-Nasir Faraj
an-nasir-faraj.summary: Sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate from 1399 to 1412, becoming ruler at just 13; his reign was marked by chaos, Timur's invasions, and rebellions, and he was assassinated in 1412.

timur.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
timur.summary: Turco-Mongol conqueror (1320s–1405) who founded the Timurid Empire across Central Asia and the Middle East, seen as one of history's greatest and most brutal military leaders.

hama.name: Hama
hama.summary: A city on the Orontes River in west-central Syria, known for its historic water-wheels (norias) and cheesemaking tradition.

abulfeda.name: Abu al-Fida
abulfeda.summary: Kurdish geographer, historian, Ayyubid prince and governor of Hama under Mamluk rule (1273–1331).

al-afdal-muhammad.name: Al-Afdal Muhammad
al-afdal-muhammad.summary: Last Ayyubid governor of Hama in Syria, reigning 1332-1341, son of the geographer Abu'l-Fida, deposed by the Mamluks.

ismailism.name: Ismailism
ismailism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, one of three alongside Twelver and Zaydi Islam, marked by its distinctive emphasis on the esoteric, hidden meaning of Islamic teaching.

qasr-ibrim.name: Qasr Ibrim
qasr-ibrim.summary: Archaeological site in Lower Nubia, Egypt, occupied from the 8th century BC to 1813, once a Nile-side city later turned into an island by the flooding from the Aswan High Dam.

al-qalqashandi.name: al-Qalqashandi
al-qalqashandi.summary: A medieval Arab Egyptian encyclopedist, polymath and mathematician (1355/56–1418) who worked as a clerk in the Mamluk chancery in Cairo and wrote the vast administrative encyclopedia Subh al-A'sha.

funj-sultanate.name: Funj Sultanate
funj-sultanate.summary: An Islamic kingdom in what is now Sudan, founded in 1504 by Sultan Amara Dunqas at its capital Sennar, reaching its peak in the late 17th century before an 1821 Turco-Egyptian conquest ended it.

berber-sudan.name: Berber, Sudan
berber-sudan.summary: A town in Sudan's River Nile state, about 50 km north of Atbara, near where the Atbara River meets the Nile.

mero.name: Meroë
mero.summary: An ancient city on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kush from around 590 BC until its collapse in the 4th century AD.

order-of-assassins.name: Assassins
order-of-assassins.summary: Member of the Nizari Isma'ili military order founded in 1090, based in mountain fortresses in Persia and Syria, known for carrying out targeted killings of rivals during the Crusades era.

butana.name: Butana
butana.summary: A region between the Atbara River and the Nile in Sudan, historically called the "Island of Meroë" when part of the Kushitic kingdom of Meroë.

gezira-scheme.name: The Gezira
gezira-scheme.summary: Region in Sudan between the Blue and White Nile rivers, named for the Arabic word for "island" and later home to one of the world's largest irrigation schemes.

kordofan.name: Kordofan
kordofan.summary: Region and former province of central Sudan, later divided in 1994 into North, South and West Kordofan states.
